sections.label: Presumption of genuine legislation
sections.summary: Clause 6 requires the Court to presume the genuineness of legislation on official websites and law reports on official or authoritative websites.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Clause 6 of the Bill extends this presumption by requiring the Court to presume the genuineness of (a) any legislation that is published on an official legislation website; and (b) any law report published on a website that publishes official or authoritative reports of decisions of the courts of a country.

sections.label: Family Court appeal restrictions
sections.summary: The Bill amends the Family Justice Act to restrict appeals from the Family Court to the High Court where specified orders are made.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: The Bill amends the Family Justice Act to restrict the right of appeal from the Family Court to the High Court, where any order specified in the new Second Schedule is made by the Family Court.

sections.label: Family proceedings start in Family Court
sections.summary: The Bill makes current practice law that family proceedings must commence in the Family Court, except classes directed by the Chief Justice to the Family Division.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: The Bill makes this current practice law by providing that all family proceedings must be commenced in the Family Court at first instance, except those classes of family proceedings which the Chief Justice has directed to be heard and determined by the Family Division of the High Court.

sections.label: Minister may designate appeal hearers
sections.summary: Clauses 10, 19, 25, 30 and 32 empower the Minister for Home Affairs to designate other MHA political officeholders to hear appeals under five Acts.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Clauses 10, 19, 25, 30 and 32 amend the Immigration Act, Massage Establishments Act, Passports Act, Private Security Industry Act and Public Entertainments and Meetings Act respectively, to empower the Minister for Home Affairs to designate other political officeholders of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to hear appeals under these Acts in his place.

sections.label: Legal Profession and Academy amendments
sections.summary: Clauses 16 and 38 make three sets of amendments on SILE rules, UniSIM Law School establishment, and referrals by the Presiding Judges.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Turning now to the amendments to the Legal Profession Act and the Singapore Academy of Law Act, clauses 16 and 38 of the Bill contain three main sets of amendments to both Acts, namely: (a) to allow the Singapore Institute of Legal Education (SILE) to enact rules for the administration of the Part A course and examinations; (b) to deal with the establishment of the new Law School of SIM University (UniSIM Law School); and (c) to allow the Presiding Judge of the Family Courts and the Presiding Judge of the State Courts to refer matters to the Law Society or the Disciplinary Tribunal.

sections.label: UniSIM law degrees recognised
sections.summary: The recently established UniSIM Law School's law degrees will be recognised for admission to the Singapore Bar, similar to NUS and SMU degrees.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Second, the UniSIM Law School was recently established, and its law degrees will be recognised for the purposes of admission to the Singapore Bar, similar to those from the National University of Singapore (NUS) and the Singapore Management University (SMU).

sections.label: Court power to rectify wills
sections.summary: Clause 50 amends the Wills Act to let Courts order rectification of a will where clerical error or failure to understand the testator's instructions defeats the testator's intentions.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Clause 50 of the Bill amends the Wills Act to expressly confer our Courts with the power to order rectification of a will upon application of any interested person.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: The Court may exercise this power where it is satisfied that the will fails to carry out the testator's intentions due to a clerical error or a failure to understand the testator's instructions.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: This amendment will allow the Courts to better give effect to the testator's testamentary intention.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: It arises from a recent decision of the Court of Appeal, which strongly suggested that the power to rectify wills is not available to our Courts.

sections.label: New section 28 rectification
sections.summary: New section 28 lets a Court order a will rectified if it fails to carry out the testator's intention due to clerical error, failure to understand instructions, or both.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The new section 28 will allow a Court to order that a will be rectified if the Court is satisfied that the will is expressed in such a way that it fails to carry out the testator's intention due to a clerical error or a failure to understand the testator's instructions, or both.

sections.label: Court rectified wills by replacement
sections.summary: The court exercised the statutory power under the Administration of Justice Act to rectify the wills by replacing each will's words with the other spouse's will.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What the court did in that case was to exercise the statutory power under the Administration of Justice Act to rectify the wills by replacing wholesale the words of each will with the text of the other spouse's will.

sections.label: Minister may exempt lawyers
sections.summary: Clauses 16(t) and (u) let the Minister make rules exempting lawyers from disciplinary action for giving gratifications or remuneration to those who procure business.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under clauses 16(t) and (u), the Minister may make rules to exempt lawyers from disciplinary action if they had given gratifications or remuneration to those who procure business for themselves or other lawyers under circumstances to be prescribed in the rules.

sections.label: Shrinking middle category lawyers
sections.summary: Statistics as at 31 August 2015 show 423 middle category lawyers against 1,909 junior and 2,502 senior lawyers, and the Bill amends about 51 Acts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Based on statistics obtained from the Law Society of Singapore, as at 31 August 2015, there are only 423 middle category lawyers, as compared to 1,909 junior lawyers and 2,502 senior lawyers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It would appear that the proposed changes to the middle category of lawyers from five to 15 years, instead of the current seven to 12 years, will go some way towards evening out the numbers of lawyers within the various categories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Senior Minister of State share the possible underlying causes which have resulted in the legal profession seeing a shrinking middle category of lawyers and whether sufficient steps are being taken to address this concern within the legal profession?

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: This Bill seeks to make several amendments to about 51 Acts, most of which are mainly technical in nature.

sections.label: Commissioner paying compensation to dependants
sections.summary: The substituted section 22(2) lets the Commissioner receive and pay compensation or interest to an employee's dependants where the employee lacks capacity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: I note that the amendment to this Act states that section 22(2) of the Act has been deleted and the following has been substituted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: It says: "Where it appears to the Commissioner that compensation or interest is payable to an employee under this Act and the employee lacks capacity within the meaning of the Mental Capacity Act, before such payment is made, it is lawful for the Commissioner to receive and pay the compensation or interest to any one or more of the dependants of the employee for the benefit of the employee, even if there is no donee of a Lasting Power of Attorney which is granted by the employee under the Mental Capacity Act and under which the employee confers on the donee authority to receive the compensation or interest, and even if there is no deputy who is appointed or deemed to be appointed for the employee by the Court under the Mental Capacity Act and who is conferred power to receive compensation or interest".

sections.label: Claimant to Commissioner of Labour
sections.summary: A question asks the Senior Minister of State to clarify who may rightly claim to the Commissioner of Labour and whether the next-of-kin's or dependant's decision is final and binding.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: Could the Senior Minister of State clarify who would be the rightful person to make a claim to the Commissioner of Labour and whether that decision made by the next-of-kin or dependant is final and binding on the employee's dependant because the law and the case law seem to say something differently?

sections.label: WICA donees and deputies
sections.summary: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked whether next-of-kin who are not donees or deputies may claim to the Commissioner of Labour and what happens if the Commissioner errs on a donee or deputy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan raised two queries on the amendments to the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA): first, whether next-of-kin who are not donees or deputies may submit claims to the Commissioner of Labour; and second, what happens if the Commissioner of Labour errs in his assessment as to whether there is a donee or deputy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I should clarify at the outset that the purpose of this particular amendment to WICA in this Bill is simply to ensure that donees have the same standing as deputies under the Act.

sections.label: Rectification of wills amendment
sections.summary: The amendment responds to the Court of Appeal's obiter holding in Cheo Yeo and Associates that rectification of wills is unavailable, giving Courts power to correct clerical errors or give effect to the testator's intention.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: What is driving this amendment was the Singapore Court of Appeal's decision in Cheo Yeo and Associates and another where the Court of Appeal held obiter that the remedy of rectification of wills is not available in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Court of Appeal's decision strongly suggested that where a will fails to embody the intentions of the testator due to a clerical error or a failure to understand the testator's intention, the Singapore Courts do not have the power to correct the error in the will.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This particular amendment was intended to address that and to give the Court the power to correct a clerical error or to give effect to the testator's intention where there was a failure to understand that intention.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: With respect to costs, that is really just intended to bring the position with respect to the Government in alignment with that for other parties in normal civil proceedings, and the costs remains at the discretion of the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: It is not intended to give the Government any additional power but just to bring it in line with other normal civil proceedings.

sections.label: Costs for more than two counsel
sections.summary: The speaker has grave reservations about the clause but says it is not intended to be oppressive and lets the Court allow costs for more than two counsel where appropriate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I have my grave reservations about this clause for the reasons I stated earlier.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, it is not intended to be used in an oppressive manner but really where if costs are incurred, it gives the Court the discretion to allow costs for more than two counsel, if the Court really thinks that this is an appropriate case to do so.

sections.label: Courts rectifying wills
sections.summary: The intention was to ensure Courts have power to rectify a clerical error or give effect to the testator's intention, with regard to the Court of Appeal's case.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: What I can say is that we had specific regard to our Court of Appeal's case and, the intention, as I had indicated, was to make sure that our Courts have the power to rectify a clerical error or our Courts have the power to give effect to the testator's intention.

sections.label: Court discretion on counsel costs
sections.summary: Where much work was incurred and it appears fair and just, the Court may award costs for more than two counsel, and if inequitable, it is up to the Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The idea is that if it is a case that really a lot of work was incurred, and it appears to the Court that it is fair and just to award costs for more than two counsel in such a situation, the Court can do so; but if the Court, having taken into account the circumstances of the case, feels that it is not equitable to do so, then it will be up to the Court.

sections.label: Reservation on legal cost clause
sections.summary: A Member records grave reservations about a clause, saying the Government could have made clear it does not use legal cost as a deterrent, but does not oppose the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Notwithstanding what the Senior Minister of State has said about the Courts being a safeguard, I do feel that the Government could have taken a different view to make it clear that it would not want to be seen to be, in a sense, using legal cost as a deterrent or prohibitive factor when it comes to litigation with the Government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: So, I want to record my reservation about that clause.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I note that the Bill is very broad-ranging, and I will not oppose the Bill, but I have grave reservations about that clause.

sections.label: Intimidation and litigation costs
sections.summary: The passage states that intimidation of Singaporeans does not spell well for Singapore's future and that the Government does not intend to use costs to intimidate anyone.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, the sense of intimidation of Singaporeans, I think, does not spell well for the future of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: It is not the intention of the Government to be using costs to intimidate anyone.
